subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum simulation
motivation: In 1998 Jaksch, Bruder, Cirac, Gardiner and Zoller showed that ultracold bosons in optical lattices realize the Bose-Hubbard model, with a tunable superfluid-Mott insulator transition. This turned Feynman's idea of a quantum simulator into a concrete experimental program. Cirac and Zoller also laid the conceptual foundations of controlled quantum many-body systems, including the ion-trap quantum computer. In 2002 Bloch and co-workers observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition. This established atoms in optical lattices as programmable quantum matter. Bloch's group went on to develop quantum gas microscopy, many-body localization and studies of Fermi-Hubbard magnetism. The program opened a new way of doing physics: strongly correlated phases, non-equilibrium dynamics and topological matter are now built and probed atom by atom. Laboratories worldwide have adopted the platform, and it links condensed-matter physics with quantum information science. It is the direct precursor of today's programmable quantum simulators and neutral-atom quantum processors.
